[[Category:Learning]]
'''Observational learning''' is the process through which [[living organism]]s acquire a behaviour by observing another organism performing the behaviour.

== Conscious observational learning ==

[[File:Spider monkey drinking plastic water bottle.png|thumbnail|]]
Conscious observational learning happens when

* '''Attention''': An organism (the '''learner''') observes another one (the '''model''') perform a task
* '''Motivation''': The learner is somehow '''motivated''' to replicate the model
** e.g., when the learner witness the model receiving [[reinforcement]]
* '''Replication''': The learner attempts, and is able to fully or partially '''replicate''' the performance of the model.

== Subconscious observational learning ==

'''Subconscious observational learning''' happens after repeated exposure to a '''model behaviour'''

* possibly without/against conscious will of the learner
* possibly without the learner's knowledge

=== Experimental evidence ===

==== Abusive behaviour inheritance ====

According to estimates cited by the Children's Bureau, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, about one-third of children grown up in households known to be abusive were identified as abusive when they became parents themselves.<ref>{{#cite:Q3504}}</ref> Assuming children do not intent to recreate their abusive childhood households as adults, '''subconscious observational learning''' must have happened in absence of their conscious motivation.

==== Exposure to violence and propensity to commit violence ====

[[File:Video game violence.png|thumbnail|Yes, violence in video game can translates into real-life violence!<ref>{{#cite:Q3519}}</ref>]]
[[Source:Violent video game effects on aggression, empathy, and prosocial behavior in Eastern and Western countries: A meta-analytic review (Scholarly article)|name-author]] causally linked exposure to violent video games with an increased propensity to commit violence.<ref>{{#cite:Q3519}}</ref>[[Source:SPSSI research summary on media violence (Scholarly article)|name-author]] further suggests a correlation between exposure to media violence (witnessing violence via television, films, or video games) and desensitisation to real-life violence, characterised by a decrease in empathy and physiological reactivity.<ref>{{#cite:Q3512}}</ref>
